description_full: Science Applications International Corporation provides technical, engineering, and mission and enterprise information technology (IT) services in the United States. It operates through two segments, Defense and Intelligence; and Civilian. The company offers IT modernization services for defense, intelligence, and civilian agencies; digital engineering services; artificial intelligence (AI) solutions; mission systems support and advisory; training and simulation; and ground vehicle support services for the nation's armed forces. It also provides services for the design, development, integration, deployment, management and operations, sustainability, and security of IT infrastructure; mission IT solutions comprising CJADC2, data and AI, digital transformation, and quantum technologies; enterprise IT solutions consisting of service management, cloud, cybersecurity, and digital workplace; engineering services, including system integration and delivery services; and professional services, such as program management. The company serves military forces, including the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marines, Coast Guard, and Space Force; agencies of the Department of War, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, U.S. Department of State, Department of Justice, and Department of Homeland Security; and members of the Intelligence Community, as well as civilian markets, such as federal, state, and local governments. The company was formerly known as SAIC Gemini, Inc. and changed its name to Science Applications International Corporation in September 2013. Science Applications International Corporation was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in Reston, Virginia.

financial_summary: Science Applications Internatio is a mid-cap technology business with a $6.1B market cap on $7.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $577M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.70× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 5.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 8.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.31x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-11.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 39% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 0.60, it is more defensive than the market.
About $54.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 46% in the 2020 crash and 15% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 46% below its DCF fair value of $272, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $188 to $404 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 17.1 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 11.6 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 10.6 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $133 on average, 9% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.38).
It converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.70x.
ROE of 24% is amplified by 3.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.2x net debt to EBITDA ($182.0M of cash against $2.5B of debt), with interest covered 5.2x.
Goodwill makes up 55% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.0% over 3 years, 0.6% over 5 years and 5.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 92% of profits supports about 11.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -4.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.96 and a backlog worth 65% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 0.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (2 purchases, net $142K bought).
It returns 8.0% a year to shareholders (6.9% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, though it has been cut 4.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 23,000 employees, each generates about $316K of revenue, 0.8x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 4.5% a year.
That works out to $25K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $783K (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
